# CHAPTER V

BERLIN (1858-1859)

A fourth child has the strength of his weakness. Being of no great value, he may throw himself away if he likes, and never be missed. Charles Francis Adams felt no love for Europe, which unfitted Americans for America—though a captious critic might have replied that all the success he or his father or his grandfather achieved was chiefly due to the field that Europe gave them. Parents are more timid for their children than for themselves; Mr. and Mrs. Adams would have kept their sons forever in Mount Vernon Street could they have relied on the moral influences of Boston itself. The boy Henry was well behaved when any one was looking at him; his moral principles, if he had any, were not known to be bad. When he presented his request to begin at a German university the study of the Civil Law—although neither he nor they knew what the Civil Law was, or any reason for his studying it—the parents dutifully consented, and walked with him down to the railway-station at Quincy to bid him good-bye, with a smile which he almost thought a tear.

He sailed in November, 1858, on the Persia. On the third day the world ran into a heavy storm. He learned then a lesson that stood by him better than any university teaching ever did—the meaning of a November gale on the mid-Atlantic. How many impressions could be crowded into one day without making any education at all became the pons asinorum of tourist mathematics.

Liverpool's November murk gave way to the romance of Chester and red-sandstone architecture. At Eaton Hall the boys were awed as Thackeray or Dickens would have felt in the presence of a Duke. Aristocracy was real. So was the England of Dickens; Oliver Twist and Little Nell lurked in every churchyard shadow, not as shadow but alive. Then came Birmingham and the Black District—the plunge into darkness lurid with flames; the sense of unknown horror in this weird gloom which never had existed before, except in volcanic craters. The boy had no idea that Karl Marx was standing there waiting for him, and that sooner or later the process of education would have to deal with Karl Marx much more than with Professor Bowen of Harvard or his Satanic free-trade majesty John Stuart Mill. The boy ran away from it, as he ran away from everything he disliked.

London was still London—heavy, clumsy, arrogant, purse-proud, but not cheap; insular but large; absolutely self-confident. History muttered down Fleet Street, like Dr. Johnson, in Adams's ear; the most insolent structures in the world were the Royal Exchange and the Bank of England. It was the London of the eighteenth century that an American felt and hated.

Education went backward. He liked it best when he hated it. The next step took it back to the sixteenth century. He crossed to Antwerp. As the Baron Osy steamed up the Scheldt in the morning mists, a travelling band on deck began to play, and groups of peasants dropped their tools to join in dancing. Ostade and Teniers were as much alive as they ever were, and even the Duke of Alva was still at home. The taste of the town was mediæval, so that Rubens seemed modern. He merely got drunk on his emotions. He was only too happy to feel himself kneeling at the foot of the Cross; he learned only to loathe the sordid necessity of getting up again, and going about his stupid business.

Dropped into Berlin one morning without guide or direction, the young man in search of education floundered in a mess of misunderstandings. A week's experience left him dazed and dull. Faith held out, but the paths grew dim. Within a day or two he was running about to beer-cellars and dance-rooms, smoking bad tobacco, drinking poor beer, and eating sauerkraut as though he knew no better. The trouble came when he asked for the education he was promised. His friends registered him at the university, selected his professors, showed him where to buy the Institutes of Gaius, and led him to his first lecture.

What Berlin's Gymnasium and university failed to teach, an accidental afternoon in a beer-hall did: amid stale tobacco and Hausfrauen knitting, Beethoven's symphonic line stole into Adams's unconscious and opened a sense he had not known he possessed, even as the German drill on memory taught him its hard limits.
